items.stem: Describe the steps of decomposition and the factors that affect its rate.
items.answer: Fragmentation: detritivores such as earthworms break detritus into smaller particles. Leaching: water-soluble nutrients go down into the soil and precipitate as unavailable salts. Catabolism: bacterial and fungal enzymes degrade detritus into simple inorganic substances. Humification: accumulation of humus, dark and resistant to microbes. Mineralisation: degradation of humus releases inorganic nutrients. Rate is controlled by chemical composition (slower with lignin and chitin, faster with nitrogen and sugars) and climatic factors (warm and moist favour it; low temperature and anaerobiosis inhibit it).
items.markingKey: 3 marks steps; 2 marks factors.

items.stem: Describe the life cycle of Plasmodium with the help of a labelled diagram. Why does a malarial patient get high fever at regular intervals?
items.answer: Sporozoites enter human blood through the bite of an infected female Anopheles; they multiply asexually in liver cells, then attack RBCs, multiplying and rupturing them; gametocytes develop in RBCs. When a female Anopheles bites, gametocytes enter the mosquito, fertilisation and development occur in the gut wall, and sporozoites gather in salivary glands. Rupture of RBCs releases haemozoin, which causes chills and high fever every 3–4 days.
items.markingKey: 2 marks human phase; 1.5 marks mosquito phase; 1.5 marks diagram and fever.

items.stem: List five reasons for which transgenic animals are produced, with an example for each where possible.
items.answer: (i) Normal physiology and development – e.g. insulin-like growth factor. (ii) Study of disease – models for cancer, cystic fibrosis, rheumatoid arthritis, Alzheimer's. (iii) Biological products – α-1-antitrypsin for emphysema; Rosie's milk with human alpha-lactalbumin (2.4 g/L). (iv) Vaccine safety – transgenic mice for polio vaccine. (v) Chemical safety testing (toxicity testing) – animals more sensitive to toxic substances give results in less time.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each reason with example.

items.stem: Discuss the evidences of evolution from palaeontology, comparative anatomy (homology and analogy), and biochemical/molecular similarity, with one example each.
items.answer: Palaeontology: fossils in rock layers of different ages show extinct forms and changes over time (e.g. dinosaurs). Homology: forelimbs of whales, bats, cheetahs and humans have similar bones – divergent evolution. Analogy: wings of butterflies and birds – convergent evolution. Biochemical: similarities in proteins and genes among diverse organisms indicate common ancestry. Also industrial melanism and resistance to pesticides as evidence of natural selection.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each for five evidences with examples.
